title: The Relational Data Model and Constraints

questions.prompt: In the relational model, what is a domain?
choices: A set of constraints that connects several relation schemas
The current set of tuples stored under a relation name
A list of attributes that describes a relation's structure
A named set of atomic values that an attribute may legally take
questions.explanation: A domain is a set of atomic values, commonly specified with a name, data type, and format. A relation schema describes attributes, while a relation state contains tuples (§5.1).

questions.prompt: In the relational model, which formal term matches each table part: a row, a column heading, and the table as a whole?
choices: Domain, relation, attribute
Attribute, tuple, domain
Tuple, attribute, relation
Relation, domain, tuple
questions.explanation: A row is a tuple, a column heading is an attribute, and the table-like collection is a relation. A domain instead describes the allowed values for an attribute (§5.1).

questions.prompt: A university adds a student row and later changes that student's GPA, but the relation's attributes remain the same. Which description fits these changes?
choices: The relation state changes while its schema stays the same
The relation degree changes while the current tuples stay fixed
The relation schema changes while its state stays the same
The domain changes while the relation schema is replaced
questions.explanation: The relation state is the current set of tuples and changes as the represented world changes; the schema is its relatively stable structure. Adding or changing rows alone does not change the attributes (§5.1).

questions.prompt: For STUDENT(Name, Ssn, Home_phone, Address, Office_phone, Age, Gpa), what is the relation's degree?
choices: 7, the number of attributes in the schema
The number of tuples currently stored in the relation
The number of possible combinations in all domains
The number of distinct domains used by the attributes
questions.explanation: The degree, also called arity, is the number of attributes in the relation schema, which is seven here. Tuple count describes the current state and is not the degree (§5.1).

questions.prompt: A STUDENT table is displayed with its rows sorted by age instead of by name. Under the relational model, what follows?
choices: It is the same relation only if the tuples are sorted by the primary key
Tuple order is undefined, so the relation is unchanged and has no semantic effect
It is a different relation because tuple order is part of the state
It is a different schema because row order changed the attribute list
questions.explanation: A relation is a set of tuples, and set elements have no order. A display or file can impose a row order, but that ordering is not part of the relation definition (§5.1).

questions.prompt: Two records list the same attribute-value pairs, but in different sequences: (Name, Kim), (Age, 20) and (Age, 20), (Name, Kim). Under the alternative mapping view of tuples, how should they be treated?
choices: As the same tuple only when the relation has exactly two attributes
As different tuples because value order must always be preserved
As different tuples unless their domains happen to be identical
Same tuple: values remain paired with their attributes
questions.explanation: Viewing a tuple as a mapping makes the order of attribute-value pairs irrelevant as long as each value stays paired with its attribute. Ordered notation is a compact alternative (§5.1).

questions.prompt: Which statements describe the basic relational model’s atomic-value (1NF) assumption? Select all that apply.
choices: A multivalued attribute is represented using separate relations
A composite attribute is represented by its simple component attributes
A value is treated as indivisible within the model
Every relation must be stored with its tuples sorted by key
questions.explanation: The basic model treats tuple values as atomic and represents multivalued attributes in separate relations and composite attributes through their simple components. Sorting tuples by key is not a relational requirement (§5.1).

questions.prompt: A STUDENT row has NULL for Office_phone because that student has no office, and another has NULL for Home_phone because the value is not known. Which meanings of NULL are represented? Select all that apply.
choices: A value exists but is unavailable
An attribute does not apply to the tuple
Two tuples' NULL values represent the same value
A value is unknown, such as the student’s home phone
questions.explanation: NULL can represent a value that is unknown, unavailable, or inapplicable. The prompt includes unknown and inapplicable cases; two NULLs do not imply equal underlying values (§5.1).

questions.prompt: Suppose `STUDENT(Name, Ssn)` is interpreted as a predicate and its current relation contains exactly the facts for Ada and Bo. Under the closed-world assumption, how is a proposed fact for Cy treated if it is absent from the relation?
choices: Invalid, because predicates cannot represent facts about entities
True, because any tuple matching the schema satisfies the predicate
False; absent facts are false under the closed-world assumption
Unknown, because the absence of a row is represented by NULL
questions.explanation: Under the closed-world assumption, the facts in the relation extension are the true facts; an absent combination makes the predicate false. A relation can represent entity facts as well as relationship facts (§5.1).

questions.prompt: Which are the three broad categories used to classify relational database constraints? Select all that apply.
choices: Schema-based constraints expressible in the data definition language
Physical storage constraints imposed by tuple display order
Inherent constraints of the data model
Application-based semantic constraints or business rules
questions.explanation: Relational constraints can be inherent to the model, schema-based, or application-based semantic rules. Physical tuple display order is not a constraint category (§5.2).

questions.prompt: A GPA attribute uses a domain defined as real numbers from 0 through 4. Which value violates its domain constraint?
choices: A superkey cannot include a name attribute
questions.explanation: A domain constraint requires an attribute value to come from that attribute's domain, including its specified type and range. 4.2 is outside the allowed range (§5.2.1).

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a key from a superkey?
choices: A key identifies multiple tuples in the relation.
A key is a minimal superkey: removing any attribute loses uniqueness in the relation.
A key may identify several tuples; a superkey must identify exactly one.
A key can contain multiple attributes; a superkey must contain one.
questions.explanation: Both keys and superkeys uniquely identify tuples. A key is minimal, meaning no attribute can be removed while preserving uniqueness; a superkey need not be minimal (§5.2.2).

questions.prompt: If a relation has more than one key, what are those keys called, and how is one commonly selected?
choices: They are relation states; one is designated as the schema key
They are foreign keys; one is designated as the superkey
They are unique keys; one is designated as the domain key
Candidate keys; one is designated the primary key
questions.explanation: Each key of a relation schema is a candidate key, and it is common to designate one candidate key as the primary key. The choice is somewhat arbitrary, though a compact key is often preferred (§5.2.2).

questions.prompt: In STUDENT, assume Ssn alone is guaranteed to uniquely identify every student. Is {Ssn, Name} a key, a superkey that is not a key, or neither?
choices: A key, because adding Name makes the identifier more specific
Neither, because a superkey cannot contain a name attribute
Superkey, but not a key; Ssn alone is unique
Neither, because two attributes are required for every superkey
questions.explanation: Because the set includes Ssn, it remains unique and is therefore a superkey. It is not minimal, since removing Name leaves the still-unique {Ssn} set (§5.2.2).

questions.prompt: STUDENT has primary key `Ssn` and an explicitly declared `NOT NULL` constraint on `Name`. A proposed tuple has NULL for both fields. Which constraints are violated? Select all that apply.
choices: Entity integrity for the primary key Ssn
Referential integrity fails because Name is NULL
The NOT NULL constraint on Name
Tuple order is violated by the missing values
questions.explanation: The declared NOT NULL rule forbids NULL in Name, and entity integrity forbids NULL in a primary key. Referential integrity concerns foreign-key references, while tuple ordering is not a constraint on NULLs (§5.2.2, §5.2.4).

questions.prompt: A relational database schema S lists relation schemas and integrity constraints. At noon, a database state DB lists the current tuple sets for those relations and satisfies those constraints. Which description is correct?
choices: S and DB are interchangeable names for an individual relation schema
S is the schema; DB is a valid current state
S is the current tuple set; DB is the structure and constraint set
S and DB are both current tuple sets, but only DB has a primary key
questions.explanation: A relational database schema consists of the relation schemas and integrity constraints; a database state consists of current relation states satisfying those constraints. A violating state would not be valid (§5.2.3).

questions.prompt: In a relational schema, EMPLOYEE.Ssn is a primary key and EMPLOYEE.Dno references DEPARTMENT.Dnumber. The current department numbers are 1, 4, and 5. Which constraints would inserting the displayed EMPLOYEE values violate?
choices: Key uniqueness, because Ssn duplicates a non-NULL key value
Domain integrity, because 7 is not an integer value
Referential integrity, because Dno 7 has no matching department
Entity integrity, because the primary-key value Ssn is NULL
questions.explanation: A primary key cannot be NULL, violating entity integrity, and Dno must match an existing department key or be NULL, so 7 violates referential integrity. The prompt gives no duplicate Ssn, and 7 can be an integer in its domain (§5.2.4).

questions.prompt: If the foreign-key attributes have compatible domains with the referenced primary key, what rule governs each foreign-key value in the referencing relation?
choices: A foreign-key value may reference several primary-key tuples
It must share the referenced primary-key attribute's name
Its value must be unique in the referencing relation
It matches a referenced primary-key value or is NULL when allowed
questions.explanation: A foreign-key value must either equal a primary-key value in a tuple of the referenced relation or be NULL; the foreign-key attributes also have compatible domains with the primary key. It need not have the same name (§5.2.4).

questions.prompt: `EMPLOYEE.Super_ssn` references `EMPLOYEE.Ssn` and stores the supervisor’s identifier. What relationship does this self-referencing foreign key represent?
choices: A foreign key from EMPLOYEE back to EMPLOYEE.Ssn
A foreign key from EMPLOYEE to DEPARTMENT.Dnumber
A candidate key formed from EMPLOYEE.Ssn and Dno
A domain constraint that limits the number of supervisors
questions.explanation: A supervisor is represented by another EMPLOYEE tuple, so Super_ssn is a self-referencing foreign key to EMPLOYEE's Ssn primary key. Dno instead references DEPARTMENT (§5.2.4).

questions.prompt: Which are examples of semantic integrity constraints, meaning application-specific business rules? Select all that apply.
choices: Salary must not exceed the supervisor’s
Weekly project hours may not exceed 56
The EMPLOYEE Ssn key cannot be NULL
Salary must use its declared numeric domain
questions.explanation: The salary-versus-supervisor rule and 56-hour weekly maximum are given as semantic integrity examples. Primary-key non-null and value-domain requirements are schema-based constraints (§5.2.5).

questions.prompt: A company requires that an employee's salary may only increase over time. What type of constraint is this?
choices: A referential-integrity constraint between employees
A domain constraint on each salary value
An entity-integrity constraint on the employee's key
A transition constraint
questions.explanation: A rule governing how the database may change from one state to another is a transition constraint. A state constraint instead limits what values are valid in a state (§5.2.5).

questions.prompt: Which three basic operations can modify relation states in the relational model?
choices: Read, Commit, and Roll Back
Select, Project, and Join
Insert, Delete, and Update
Create, Describe, and Sort
questions.explanation: Insert adds tuples, Delete removes tuples, and Update or Modify changes attribute values in existing tuples. Select, Project, and Join are retrieval operations (§5.3).

questions.prompt: Assume `EMPLOYEE.Dno` is a foreign key referencing `DEPARTMENT.Dnumber`, and no DEPARTMENT row has Dnumber 7. What happens to referential integrity if an EMPLOYEE tuple with Dno 7 is inserted?
choices: It is satisfied because foreign keys need only use the same data type
It is violated because Dno has no matching department key under referential integrity
It is satisfied because Dno is not part of the EMPLOYEE primary key
It is violated only if the employee's Super_ssn is also non-NULL
questions.explanation: EMPLOYEE.Dno references DEPARTMENT.Dnumber, so a non-NULL Dno must match an existing department primary-key value. Merely having a compatible type does not satisfy referential integrity (§5.3.1).

questions.prompt: An Insert operation violates an integrity constraint. What is the usual default response, and what may the DBMS do to help?
choices: Convert the violating value to NULL without notifying the user
Accept the insertion, then mark the resulting database state as invalid
Delete the referencing relation and ask the user to recreate it
Reject it; the DBMS may explain the violation or request a correction
questions.explanation: The default is to reject an insertion that violates constraints; the DBMS could provide a reason or ask the user to correct the value. Automatically accepting an invalid state is not the described response (§5.3.1).

questions.prompt: Assume `WORKS_ON.Essn` is a foreign key referencing `EMPLOYEE.Ssn`. What constraint issue results from deleting the employee shown in the data?
choices: Key integrity, because the remaining employee keys become non-unique
Entity integrity, because deleting a tuple makes its former key NULL
Referential integrity: WORKS_ON retains a dangling reference
Domain integrity, because a value disappears from the Ssn domain
questions.explanation: Deleting the referenced EMPLOYEE tuple while the WORKS_ON foreign key still contains its Ssn would leave a dangling reference and violate referential integrity (§5.3.2).

questions.prompt: If deleting a tuple would violate referential integrity, which responses can preserve that constraint? Select all that apply.
choices: Delete referencing tuples as well (cascade)
Reject the deletion (restrict)
Reorder relation tuples, then retry deletion
Set referencing values to NULL or a valid default
questions.explanation: The described options are restrict, cascade, and setting the offending referencing values to NULL or a valid default. Reordering tuples does not resolve a referential-integrity violation (§5.3.2).

questions.prompt: EMPLOYEE.Ssn is a primary key referenced by WORKS_ON.Essn. If the employee with Ssn 111 is directly updated to Ssn 222 while another employee already has Ssn 222 and WORKS_ON still contains Essn 111, which constraints are violated? Select all that apply.
choices: Referential integrity: WORKS_ON still references Ssn 111
The domain constraint, because 222 is not an employee identifier value
Key constraint: Ssn 222 duplicates an existing key
Entity integrity, because the new Ssn is NULL
questions.explanation: The new Ssn duplicates another employee's primary key, violating the key constraint; existing WORKS_ON references to 111 also lose their referenced tuple. The new value is non-NULL and is not described as outside its domain (§5.3.3).

questions.prompt: What is a transaction in the context of a relational database?
choices: A retrieval query that always returns exactly one tuple
An atomic unit of database operations that leaves a valid state
A single Update operation that changes one attribute in one tuple
A relation schema that defines the database's primary and foreign keys
questions.explanation: A transaction is an executing program with database operations that together form an atomic unit of work; at its end, the database must satisfy its constraints. It may include multiple retrievals and updates, not just one Update (§5.3.4).
